notes: Historic Timothy Evans CCRC referral JR; discretion and pardon effect clearly reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Westlake JR: CCRC discretion not to refer historic Evans conviction
key_facts: Mary Westlake, Timothy Evans's half-sister, sought judicial review of the CCRC's refusal to refer his 1950 murder conviction to the Court of Appeal.
Evans had been executed after conviction for murdering his daughter Geraldine; Christie later confessed to killing his wife Beryl and a 1966 royal pardon exonerated him.
The CCRC accepted a real possibility the conviction would be quashed but exercised discretion not to refer, citing the pardon, publicity and compensation already paid.
The family sought referral mainly to remove any slur from the Brabin inquiry finding that Evans probably killed his wife.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of the Criminal Cases Review Commission's decision not to refer a posthumous conviction despite satisfaction of section 13 preconditions.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed with costs to the CCRC; the court nonetheless stated in open court that Evans should be regarded as innocent of both murders.
enrichment.ratio: Section 9 confers a real discretion whether to refer once section 13 is satisfied; fairness does not create a presumption of referral, especially in historic posthumous cases where a royal pardon and compensation have already vindicated innocence and referral would consume resources for limited benefit.
legal_issues: Whether there is a presumption in favour of referral once section 13 preconditions are met
Whether quashing the conviction would bring tangible benefit after a free pardon
Whether the Court of Appeal could address Brabin report findings about Beryl Evans's murder
Whether the CCRC misdirected itself on the effect of R v Foster on royal pardons
linked_authorities: R v CCRC ex parte Pearson [2000] 1 Cr.App.R 141
Clark [2001] EWCA Crim 884
R (Hunt) v Criminal Cases Review Commission [2001] 2 Cr.App.R (S) 76
Hanratty [2002] EWCA Crim 1141
R v Foster [1985] QB 115

confidence.notes: Statutory framework, CCRC reasoning and dismissal are all clearly recorded.

notes: Unless-order debarral and substantive appeal with county court retrial directions.

enrichment.short_title: Windmill Racing Stables: debarred appellant; Lewis appeal allowed for retrial
key_facts: Stephen Barnett trading as Windmill Racing Stables resisted Gerald Lewis's appeal after a county court judgment on a £2,000 payment dispute.
The Court of Appeal had ordered Barnett to disclose pleadings and documents from related Piper and Wakefield litigation by 13 July 2004; he did not comply.
At a show-cause hearing Barnett argued Ward LJ had earlier discharged a similar disclosure order and treated the June order as ineffective.
The court debarred Barnett from resisting the appeal, allowed it on the basis the claim rested on a false legal premise, and remitted for retrial with liberty to amend.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal hearing on unless-order compliance, fresh evidence applications, charging-order discharge, and the substantive appeal listed together.
enrichment.outcome: Barnett debarred from resisting the appeal; appeal allowed, recorder's order set aside, retrial ordered with amendment permission and charging/possession proceedings set aside.
enrichment.ratio: Blatant non-compliance with a clear and unequivocal disclosure order warrants enforcing an unless order debarring resistance to appeal; where a county court claim failed on a redeemable legal error, justice requires remission for retrial with permission to plead on a corrected basis rather than final disposal on the flawed claim.
legal_issues: Whether Barnett showed cause against debarral for breach of the disclosure order
Whether fresh evidence should be admitted to excuse non-compliance
Whether the substantive appeal should succeed on the legal basis of the claim
Whether charging orders should be discharged pending retrial

confidence.notes: Procedural history and final order are explicit though the underlying contract issue is not fully re-decided.

notes: Three consolidated supplier appeals on delivery to fraudster at serviced offices.

enrichment.short_title: Computer 2000 v ICM: suppliers entitled to price after fraudulent AMEC delivery
key_facts: Three computer suppliers sued ICM for goods sold and delivered under purchase orders naming AMEC Plc at South Bank House FAO Richard Cole.
A fraudster using the AMEC name rented serviced office space; security guard Bee received goods and Richard Cole collected them within minutes.
AMEC Plc had no connection with the address; the goods were lost to fraud and ICM refused to pay the suppliers.
Judge Catlin held delivery was made to the person ICM held out as authorised and dismissed ICM's non-delivery defence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated appeals to the Court of Appeal from three Reading County Court judgments refusing permission to appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed with costs; suppliers' judgments upheld including indemnity costs and interest orders against ICM for Imago.
enrichment.ratio: Where a buyer's purchase order directs delivery to a named addressee FAO a specified person, delivery to that person satisfies the seller's obligation; on Galbraith and Grant principles delivery to an apparently authorised recipient at designated premises also discharges the seller even if a fraudster misappropriates the goods.
legal_issues: Whether suppliers proved delivery in accordance with ICM purchase orders
Whether Mr Bee or Richard Cole had authority from AMEC Plc to accept delivery
Whether ICM held out Richard Cole as the person authorised to receive goods
Whether C2K's standard terms superseded ICM's conditions
linked_authorities: Galbraith and Grant Ltd v Block [1922] 2 KB 155
Freeman & Lockyer v Buckhurst Park Properties (Mangal) Ltd [1964] 2 QB 480

confidence.notes: Facts, contractual analysis and disposal on all three appeals are comprehensively reasoned.

notes: Housing benefit voluntary payment disregard under Schedule 4 paragraph 13.

enrichment.short_title: Perkins housing benefit: son's gifts disregarded under paragraph 13(2)

statutes_considered.title: Child Support, Pensions and Social Security Act 2000

key_facts: Major Perkins received housing benefit from Ryedale District Council based on pension income below the applicable threshold.
He disclosed a second bank account receiving £280 monthly gifts from his son in Australia; the council treated these as income and recovered £7,750.15.
The appeal tribunal rejected his appeal; Commissioner Rowland held paragraph 13(2) permitted full disregard where gifts were intended and used for non-basic items.
The Secretary of State appealed after not appearing before the Commissioner, arguing impermissible presumptions were applied.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Secretary of State's appeal to the Court of Appeal against a Social Security Commissioner's decision allowing Major Perkins's housing benefit appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Commissioner's decision upheld on the peculiar facts though not treated as a general precedent.
enrichment.ratio: Paragraph 13(1) allows only £20 disregard of regular voluntary payments unless paragraph 13(2) applies where payments are both intended and used for items other than food, fuel, rent or ordinary clothing; tribunals may draw case-specific inferences from evidence but must not apply general presumptions, and the Secretary of State may appeal even if he did not appear below.
legal_issues: Whether the Commissioner erred by presuming intention and use of voluntary payments
Whether the Secretary of State should be refused a hearing after non-appearance below
How paragraph 13(1) and 13(2) interact on regular gifts from a donor
Whether sufficient evidence supported disregard of the son's monthly payments
linked_authorities: Secretary of State for Work and Pensions v Hughes (A Minor) [2004] EWCA Civ 16

confidence.notes: Regulatory construction and fact-specific application are clearly explained.

notes: Restrictive covenant parking construction on Uppingham Hall Gardens roadway.

enrichment.short_title: Smith v Garrard: parking covenant construed as obstruction-based not absolute
key_facts: Martin Smith owned The Hall at Uppingham; Jeanne Garrard owned No 4 Hall Gardens with rights over a shared driveway from a 1997 transfer.
Paragraph 10 of the transfer covenant prohibited parking on the roadway over which others had rights of way.
Mrs Garrard and visitors parked alongside her property on an area shown as visitors' parking on the development plan without blocking passage.
Judge Norris awarded £100 for annoyance under paragraph 6 but refused an absolute parking injunction; Smith appealed on paragraph 10 construction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from Birmingham County Court on construction of a restrictive covenant and related costs order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; parking in the approved space without impeding rights of way did not breach paragraph 10.
enrichment.ratio: Reading paragraph 10 in context, the restriction on parking vehicles on the roadway is linked to obstruction of rights of way rather than an absolute ban; the phrase 'over which other persons have rights of way' indicates parking is prohibited only where it interferes with passage, not where it merely affects amenity.
legal_issues: Whether paragraph 10 absolutely forbids all parking on the roadway
Whether the qualifying words relate to obstruction or define the servient land
Whether approved visitors' parking on the development plan breaches the covenant
Whether the judge erred in refusing an injunction and awarding nominal damages only
linked_authorities: Investors Compensation Scheme Ltd v West Bromwich Building Society [1998] 1 WLR 896
Tea Trade Properties Ltd v CIN Properties Ltd [1991] EGLR 155

confidence.notes: Covenant text, factual parking layout and purposive construction are fully analysed.

notes: Unlimited civil proceedings order under section 42 against habitual litigant.

enrichment.short_title: Attorney General v Lewis: unlimited civil proceedings order under section 42
key_facts: The Attorney General applied for a civil proceedings order against Kess Thomas Lewis under section 42 of the Supreme Court Act 1981.
Since September 1999 Lewis had commenced over 40 sets of proceedings, almost all struck out or dismissed, repeatedly suing landlords, Tesco and public authorities.
Prior civil restraint orders had not stopped further litigation including five judicial review claims about a 1998 washing machine theft.
Lewis denied vexatious conduct, alleged racial discrimination by the courts, and immediately announced an intention to appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application by the Attorney General for a civil proceedings order after extensive litigation history summarised in a schedule.
enrichment.outcome: Section 42 civil proceedings order made with unlimited duration; permission to appeal refused from the bench.
enrichment.ratio: Section 42 requires habitual, persistent and groundless institution of vexatious civil proceedings; hallmarks include claims with little legal basis, repeated relitigation, abuse of process and refusal to accept adverse decisions, and where restraint orders have failed an unlimited order may properly follow.
legal_issues: Whether Lewis habitually and persistently instituted vexatious proceedings without reasonable ground
Whether employment tribunal proceedings could support the application
Whether the court should exercise discretion to make a civil proceedings order
What duration the order should have given prior limited restraints failed
linked_authorities: In re Vernazza [1959] 1 WLR 622
Attorney General v Barker [2000] 1 FLR 759
Attorney General v Matthews [2001] EWCA Civ 254
Attorney General v Jones [1991] W.L.R. 859

notes: Nine interlocutory applications in Teamtrend corporate control dispute.

enrichment.short_title: Shahar v Tsitsekkos: Teamtrend jurisdiction and service applications decided
key_facts: Michael Shahar claimed Kolomoisky and Cheklanov conspired to seize control of English company Teamtrend and strip Ukrainian assets held via Ged companies.
Parallel actions challenged corporate steps as invalid and sought beneficial ownership of Teamtrend shares under a June 2002 agreement.
Nine applications raised service out, Brussels Regulation jurisdiction, summary judgment, discharge of ex parte injunctions and Privatbank joinder.
Shahar held Teamtrend shares as nominee; tort and subrogation claims largely concerned conduct in Ukraine.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery hearing of nine grouped interlocutory applications in two related actions concerning Teamtrend Limited and Ukrainian asset disputes.
enrichment.outcome: Tort claims against several defendants struck out or stayed for forum non conveniens; summary judgment refused; ex parte injunctions largely maintained; service on Privatbank set aside; amendment application dismissed without being pursued.
enrichment.ratio: Tort claims depending on stripping nominee-held assets abroad do not satisfy CPR 6.20 gateways or Article 5(3) where loss occurred outside England; Ukraine is the appropriate forum; without-notice relief may survive innocent non-disclosure where balance of convenience favours retention; a completed VAT-style internal assessment analogy aside, protective service requires full material disclosure including nominee arrangements.
legal_issues: Whether tort claims fall within CPR 6.20 and the Judgments Regulation for service out
Whether England is the proper forum for conspiracy and economic tort claims
Whether summary judgment should declare corporate steps invalid
Whether Lindsay J's without-notice injunctions should be discharged for non-disclosure
Whether Privatbank was properly joined and served in Ukraine
linked_authorities: Konamaneni v Rolls Royce [2002] 1 WLR 1269
In re Banco Nacional de Cuba [2001] 1 WLR 2039

confidence.notes: Very long judgment with multiple discrete rulings; core jurisdictional holdings are clear though some corporate validity issues remain for trial.

notes: Protective VAT assessment validity after Primback litigation.

enrichment.short_title: Courts plc v HMRC: December 1999 protective VAT assessment held valid
key_facts: Courts plc accounted for VAT on retail finance sales net of finance charges following Primback in the Court of Appeal.
HMRC completed a VAT641 on 16 December 1999 for over £5.3m but did not process it, notifying Courts by letter pending the Primback appeal.
Further assessments in May and June 2000 revised figures; a November 2001 VAT641 was processed generating a duplicate VAT655 later withdrawn.
Courts argued no valid assessment was made because the officer followed internal advice and processing was omitted.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against dismissal of Courts plc's challenge to protective VAT assessments before the VAT and Duties Tribunal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; December 1999 assessment valid though figures later varied by alternative May/June 2000 assessments; November 2001 did not supersede it.
enrichment.ratio: A protective assessment under section 73 is a normal assessment once an officer exercises best judgment and records it in a completed VAT641, even if not processed to ledger; notification by letter can create an immediate debt pending Primback; later alternative assessments may reduce amounts but do not withdraw the earlier assessment unless expressly superseded.
legal_issues: Whether a decision to assess was made when the officer followed protective assessment guidance
Whether processing and issue of VAT655 is part of making an assessment
Whether December 1999 assessments were conditional and therefore invalid
Whether May/June 2000 or November 2001 assessments superseded the protective assessment
linked_authorities: Primback v Customs and Excise Commissioners [1996] STC 757
Don Pasquale v Commrs for Customs & Excise [1990] STC 556
Cheesman v Commrs for Customs & Excise [2000] STC 1119
University Court of the University of Glasgow v Customs & Excise Commrs [2003] STC 495
Pegasus Birds v Commrs for Customs & Excise [2004] EWCA 1015

notes: Judicial review of magistrates' refusal to accept company-laid assault information.

enrichment.short_title: Gladstone plc JR: company may lay common assault information at AGM
key_facts: Gladstone plc sought judicial review after a district judge held Bradley Lee had no authority to lay an information alleging Norman Guiver assaulted CEO Benjamin Merrett at an AGM.
The board resolved to pursue the shareholder resolutely and fund Merrett's prosecution costs; solicitors laid the information in the company's name.
The judge ruled only the individually aggrieved victim could prosecute and a body corporate lacked locus and authority.
Guiver, a dissenting minority shareholder, resisted as interested party; the court treated the issues as questions of law.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review with Lord Justice Rose of the district judge's ruling dismissing a common assault summons for want of prosecutorial locus.
enrichment.outcome: Decision quashed including costs ruling; information held valid; summons restored and hearing remitted; no order as to costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where an alleged assault at a public company's AGM concerns public interest in orderly governance, the company may lay an information through an authorised solicitor under rule 4(1) if its objects include managing and controlling company operations; Rubin v DPP on bodies corporate as informants need not be resolved when a natural person solicitor lays the information on the company's authority.
legal_issues: Whether Gladstone plc had locus to institute criminal proceedings for an AGM assault
Whether prosecution required the individually aggrieved victim as informant
Whether the board resolution authorised the solicitors to lay the information
Whether the challenge was properly brought by judicial review rather than case stated
linked_authorities: Rubin v DPP [1989] 2 All ER 241
R v Ealing Justices, ex parte Dixon [1990] 2 QB 91
Cole v Coulton (1860) 24 JP 596

notes: Collective agreement incorporation and no compulsory redundancy promise.

enrichment.short_title: Kaur v MG Rover: Way Ahead redundancy pledge not incorporated into contract
key_facts: Mrs Kaur, a Longbridge staff employee, faced compulsory redundancy in March 2003 and sought declarations that collective agreements barred compulsory redundancy.
Her 2000 contract incorporated Standard Conditions subject to collective agreements where appropriate, including a notice clause permitting company termination on notice.
The New Deal 1992 principles included a no-redundancy aspiration but amendments were in a separate agreement part; The Way Ahead 1997 stated 'THERE WILL BE NO COMPULSORY REDUNDANCY'.
The judge declared paragraph 2.1 of The Way Ahead incorporated and barred compulsory redundancy; MG Rover appealed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal to the Court of Appeal from a High Court declaration on incorporation of collective agreements into an individual employment contract.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed and cross-appeal dismissed; declaratory relief set aside; no contractual bar to compulsory redundancy found.
enrichment.ratio: Collective agreements are incorporated only where appropriate and the particular provision is apt for individual enforcement; The New Deal principles were aspirational and not carried into contractual amendments, and The Way Ahead paragraph 2.1 expressed a collective objective contingent on workforce co-operation rather than a binding individual term, and even if incorporated would not override an express notice termination clause without incompatible construction.
legal_issues: Whether The New Deal principles on job security were incorporated
Whether The Way Ahead paragraph 2.1 was apt for incorporation into individual contracts
Whether a no compulsory redundancy term prevails over express notice of termination provisions
How Alexander v Standard Telephones principles apply to expressly incorporated collective agreements
linked_authorities: Alexander v Standard Telephones and Cables Ltd (No. 2) [1991] IRLR 286
National Coal Board v National Union of Mineworkers [1986] IRLR 439
Johnson v Unisys Limited [2001] UKHL 13
Reda v Flag Limited [2002] UKPC 38
